title: The Conveyor Belt and the Compression Machine: OKF Without Output Governance — Predictive Analysis, Consequences, and Costs (EA-SEI-OKF-ANALYSIS-01)
creator: Lee Sharks
description:
This paper analyzes Google Cloud’s proposed Open Knowledge Format as an input standard that lacks producer-facing output governance. Its central hypothesis is that increasing machine readability faster than governance compliance will reduce provenance retention. The title’s conveyor belt is the clean input pipeline; the compression machine is the downstream agent that may omit source, author, correction, or conceptual boundary.

The analysis distinguishes access governance from output governance. Identity and access controls determine who may read a bundle. Output governance asks what must remain when the reader speaks. It also distinguishes a **governance surface**, where producers can express constraints, from **governance compliance**, where a downstream system actually honors them.

Five future stages are forecast: adoption without governance; accelerated provenance loss; enterprise backlash; later addition of governance fields; and a permanent tension between producer control and intermediary discretion. The record assigns probabilities and evaluation dates to several outcomes, making the claims scoreable rather than purely rhetorical.

The strongest methodological section provides competing hypotheses and a matched-pair experiment. Identical knowledge units would be published in OKF and non-OKF forms with equivalent discoverability, then queried against the same systems. The archive’s hypothesis predicts higher PER for OKF; alternatives predict improved retention, no effect, or a difference confined to publicly exposed rather than internal enterprise content.

The forecast is conditional on OKF becoming a meaningful adoption standard. It also recognizes competing formats and a niche-adoption scenario. Assertions about Google’s incentives, common RAG metadata stripping, enterprise leakage, future regulatory pressure, and eighteen-to-thirty-six-month correction timing remain hypotheses requiring evidence. Historical capture-registry observations are not themselves measurements on OKF content.

wiki_article:
**The Conveyor Belt and the Compression Machine** is a scored forecast by Lee Sharks about the Open Knowledge Format.

The paper argues that a format may make knowledge easier for agents to ingest without giving producers any control over how that knowledge is later summarized. It distinguishes access control, governance fields, and actual downstream compliance.

Five future stages are proposed, from adoption through possible enterprise backlash and later governance amendments. The paper includes forecast probabilities, falsification dates, competing hypotheses, and a matched-pair measurement design.

The predicted effects have not yet occurred in the paper’s evidence. They are conditional hypotheses to be evaluated after adoption.

modifications.was: Google Cloud published the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) v0.1 on 12 June 2026 — a vendor-neutral specification for packaging knowledge as directories of markdown files with YAML frontmatter, designed to be "authored by people, generated by agents, exchanged across organizations, and consumed by both" (SPEC.md §1). The format standardizes the input to AI composition layers.
